The scalp lesion fits the description of a fibrous cephalic plaque (FCP), a well-recognized TSC-associated lesion that is congenital/early-onset, firm, hairless, and histologically shows dense collagenous/connective tissue proliferation with decreased adnexal structures—findings that match the biopsy (dense collagen, fewer/distorted follicles, perifollicular fibrosis). The capillary proliferation and whorled collagen can be seen in fibrous cephalic plaque/collagenous connective tissue nevus as well.
- Alternative entities considered:
  - Connective tissue nevus (collagenoma) — histology overlaps with the biopsy (dense collagen), and clinically fits shagreen-type lesions; however the combination with facial angiofibromas and an FCP strongly favors TSC as the unifying diagnosis.
  - Nevus seb with secondary adnexal tumors (e.g., trichoblastoma) can present as a congenital hairless scalp plaque that develops papules, but expected sebaceous/epithelial adnexal changes were not seen on histology, and the presence of facial angiofibromas/shagreen patch is not explained by nevus seb alone.
  - Nodular/keloidal morphea and keloid/hypertrophic scar can produce dense collagen and whorled fibrosis, but they usually have different clinical histories (preceding inflammation/trauma or sclerodermoid changes) and do not explain the facial angiofibromas and sacral shagreen patch.

Implication
- The most parsimonious diagnosis is TSC with a fibrous cephalic plaque on the scalp (with nodular overgrowths), supported by histology and by other cutaneous TSC stigmata (facial angiofibromas, shagreen patch). Confirmation by clinical exam for other TSC findings and genetic testing (TSC1/TSC2) and appropriate systemic evaluation (brain MRI, renal imaging, cardiac/ocular review) is recommended.

[DIAGNOSIS]
1. Fibrous cephalic plaque of Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC) with nodular/collagenous overgrowth (most likely)
2. Connective tissue nevus (collagenoma) — solitary/circumscribed collagenoma (could be part of or independent from TSC)
3. Nevus sebaceus of the scalp with secondary adnexal proliferations (less likely given histology)
4. Nodular (keloidal) morphea / localized scleroderma with keloidal transformation
5. Keloid / hypertrophic scar formation within a preexisting plaque
